newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian SGB chief sees higher profit, stable div.
newsitem.headline: Belgian SGB chief sees higher profit, stable div.

text.p: Etienne Davignon, chairman of Belgian holding company Societe Generale de Belgique SA (SGB), said he expected profits to grow in 1996 and 1997 but indicated the dividend on 1996 earnings would be left unchanged.
"I can confirm our October forecast that current and net 1996 profits will rise, that is now a fact," Davignon told Reuters in an interview.
In 1995, SGB's group net profit fell 16 percent to 9.21 billion Belgian francs, mainly because of the weak economy and the fall of the dollar.
"At the moment, all our businesses are doing well. 1997 already looks better than 1996," Davignon said.

But he also indicated that SGB -- which is burdened by a 32 billion franc debt -- would keep its dividend on 1996 earnings unchanged from the 87 francs per share net paid on 1995 earnings. "I see no great reason for an increase of dividend," he said, adding that no decision on dividend had been taken yet.

"There seems to be no business reason to have an excessive payout," Davignon said, adding that SGB shares had performed well in 1996 and the total return on SGB stock was significantly higher than the interest rate on bank deposits.
Davignon also said that it was "technically possible" to consider an optional stock dividend.

Analysts have pointed out that SGB is loaded with 32 billion francs worth of debt following the increase of its stake in its Tractebel unit last year, while SGB parent company Compagnie de Suez is sitting on a cash pile of roughly the same size.
A stock dividend would be a way of keeping cash in SGB rather than moving it to Suez, which owns 62 percent of SGB.
"It is obvious that if Suez had large debts, we could not consider a stock dividend. We are now in the situation that we can look at the possibility of an optional stock dividend," Davignon said.

He stressed that no decisions had been taken yet on a dividend and said that a stock dividend had not yet been formally studied. "Every year we must study the most adequate way of paying our shareholders," he said, adding that stock dividends have been used by several SGB units in the past.
